evidence.title: When Do Physicians Trust AI? The Role of Clinical Context in Decision Support: SMART vignette study
evidence.outcome: perceived confidence and effectiveness of AI-CDSS
evidence.effect: amount of information did not significantly affect perceived confidence or effectiveness
evidence.quote: Neither clinical decision type nor amount of information significantly affected perceived confidence or effectiveness.

commentary.bottom_line: Thirteen sources endorse telling clinicians each AI tool's intended purpose, capabilities, automation level, expected accuracy, and permitted uses. One vignette study of 420 physicians found that the amount of information given did not significantly change perceived confidence or effectiveness, and no study measured whether disclosure reduces out-of-scope use.

perspectives.view: The only test is a single offline vignette simulation (n=420 physicians, United States) with a null result on perceived confidence and effectiveness. Self-reported perception is an indirect outcome, and the design did not observe actual use outside intended scope. With one study, serious indirectness, and no measure of patient outcomes, certainty that disclosure changes clinician behavior is very low.

The hazard is clinicians applying a tool beyond its validated scope. No supplied study documents how often this occurs, and the one test measured perceptions rather than errors or misuse caught before reaching patients. Whether disclosure of accuracy and non-permissible uses intercepts unsafe use therefore remains untested.

In the vignette study, giving physicians more information about an AI decision-support tool did not significantly shift their perceived confidence or effectiveness. This suggests that the volume of disclosure alone may not change how clinicians regard a tool. The study did not test format, timing, or placement of information within the clinical workflow.

The FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software lists degree of automation as information a submission may describe, and radiology societies state that transparency must include purpose, operating conditions, and expected accuracy. These are expectations of disclosure. None of the supplied endorsements cites outcome data showing that labeling of this kind prevents off-label clinical use.

The HEAAL framework states that communication should extend beyond technical specifications and intended use, and the AMA principles ask that intended population and practice setting be stated. The single test enrolled physicians in a simulated setting and reported no information on the patient populations or care settings represented in the vignettes.

commentary.research_gap: No study has measured whether informing clinicians of intended use, accuracy, and prohibited uses reduces actual out-of-scope use, diagnostic error, or patient harm in live clinical settings. Trials comparing disclosure formats and delivery points within the workflow, with observed behavior as the outcome, are needed.
commentary.underserved_note: The one test was a vignette study of physicians and reported no inclusion of Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations or settings. Whether disclosure about a tool's intended population helps clinicians avoid applying it to groups outside its validation data is untested.
